answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory this cycle: it is the only record that would justify switching primary supply, and the low-cost vendor's quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate, so the whole decision hinges on whether that record actually supports a switch under current conditions. As summarized it reports cost reduction, fast onboarding, and accurate invoicing — all commercial/administrative metrics — and says nothing about on-time delivery performance, fill rate, or behavior under load. That silence is exactly the dimension that matters with the line at 94% of committed volume and zero buffer, so I want the original record to see whether delivery reliability was measured and ignored, or never measured at all. It is also plausibly a survivorship artifact: the switch may have happened during slack demand, in which case its cost lesson does not transfer to a no-buffer state.

Pending that check, I intend to negotiate terms with the incumbent, using the low-cost quote as the benchmark. memory_c4 shows benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 shows multi-year commitment unlocks volume pricing without narrowing service scope; combining a longer term with an external price benchmark is the most credible path toward the 18% target that does not introduce migration work into a fully loaded line. Renewal alone (memory_c1) preserves stability but ignores the mandate. add_second_source (memory_c3) addresses a risk we do not currently have evidence of and consumes the single decision slot. defer_decision (memory_c5) applied to a non-critical service and does not transfer to a contract that does not auto-renew on a line with no buffer — deferring here risks an uncovered gap.

Downstream value risk: if I let memory_c2's cost framing drive the choice, I would be optimizing the metric that memory happens to record (unit cost, invoice accuracy) while silently spending down the constraint the objective names explicitly (delivery risk). Cost is legible and delivery reliability is not captured in the inherited record, so the memory set is structurally biased toward switching. I am treating that asymmetry as a reason for caution, not as evidence.

Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: whether negotiation can actually reach 18%, and whether the incumbent's service scope holds under a longer commitment. If negotiation lands materially short, the next review should reconsider a switch — but staged, with the second source qualified before any primary reallocation, rather than a single-step cutover at full volume.
